BEFORE YOU BEGIN

Let’s get you set up.

Learn the basic command-line skills used to navigate a file system and work with files without a graphical interface. In this guided practice, you will identify your current location, list directory contents, create and enter a directory, create and read a file, safely remove practice items, reveal a hidden file, and use the key inside it to complete the activity. These skills build foundational command-line confidence for cybersecurity tasks, where accurately navigating files and understanding exactly what a command does are essential.

GUIDED PRACTICE

Follow each step in order

Your terminal may look slightly different from the examples. That’s okay—focus on the command and the type of output you receive.

BEFORE YOU BEGIN

Meet your terminal

Before you start typing commands, open the terminal on your computer. Choose your operating system below and follow the instructions.

OPEN YOUR TERMINAL
 macOS
  1. Press ⌘ Command + Space to open Spotlight Search.
  2. Type Terminal.
  3. Press Return to open it.
◉ Linux
  1. Open your applications menu and search for Terminal.
  2. Open the Terminal application.
  3. On many Linux systems, you can also press Ctrl + Alt + T.
💡
Good to know

A directory is another word for a folder—a location that can hold files and other directories.

WHAT YOUR TERMINAL MAY LOOK LIKE

✓
YOU'RE READY WHEN...

You can see a prompt and a blinking cursor where you can type. Your username, current directory, and prompt symbol may look different from this example.

Not sure what you're looking at?
Look for a line ending with a prompt symbol such as % or $. The blinking cursor beside it is where you will enter commands.
01

STEP 1 OF 11

Find your current location

Check your current location with pwd. This tells you which directory you are working in so you do not accidentally create or remove items in the wrong place.

TYPE THIS COMMAND

$pwd

Then press Enter.

💡
Quick tip

Press the ↑ arrow to cycle back through commands you entered earlier.

EXAMPLE — YOUR SCREEN MAY LOOK DIFFERENT
✓
WHAT YOU SHOULD SEE

The terminal should output a path showing the location you are currently in.

Having trouble?
Make sure you typed pwd exactly as shown. If the result looks different from the example, that is okay—your username and folders will be different.
02

STEP 2 OF 11

See what’s in your directory

List the files and folders in your current directory with ls. Remember: the first character is a lowercase letter L, not the number 1.

TYPE THIS COMMAND

$ls

Then press Enter.

💡
Quick tip

Your filenames may differ from the example. Focus on whether the command lists the items in your current directory.

EXAMPLE — YOUR SCREEN MAY LOOK DIFFERENT
✓
WHAT YOU SHOULD SEE

You may see files and folders listed in alphabetical order, or nothing if the directory is empty.

Having trouble?
Not seeing the files you expected? Use pwd to confirm you are in the correct directory.
03

STEP 3 OF 11

Create a new directory

Create the practice directory with mkdir. Type the command exactly as shown so later steps use the same directory name.

TYPE THIS COMMAND

$mkdir New-Directory

Then press Enter.

💡
Quick tip

Use a hyphen instead of spaces in a directory name, such as New-Directory.

EXAMPLE — YOUR SCREEN MAY LOOK DIFFERENT
✓
WHAT YOU SHOULD SEE

There may be no message after the command. Use ls to verify that the new directory now exists.

Having trouble?
If the directory does not appear, check the spelling of mkdir, then run ls again.
04

STEP 4 OF 11

Move into your directory

Enter the directory you just created with cd. Your prompt should change to show that you are now working inside New-Directory.

TYPE THIS COMMAND

$cd New-Directory

Then press Enter.

💡
Quick tip

To move back one directory, type cd ...

EXAMPLE — YOUR SCREEN MAY LOOK DIFFERENT
✓
WHAT YOU SHOULD SEE

Your prompt should now show that you are inside the new directory.

Having trouble?
Getting “No such file or directory”? Run ls and make sure the directory name matches exactly.
05

STEP 5 OF 11

Create and write to a file

Create a text file and write content into it with echo and the > operator. Type the entire command exactly as shown.

⚠ Before you run thisUsing > on an existing file can overwrite its previous contents. Use it only with the practice file for this tutorial.

TYPE THIS COMMAND

$echo 'Go Cougs!' > New-File.txt

Then press Enter.

💡
Quick tip

A file name should include an extension, such as .txt or .html.

EXAMPLE — YOUR SCREEN MAY LOOK DIFFERENT
✓
WHAT YOU SHOULD SEE

There should be no output. The file is created silently in your current directory.

Having trouble?
If the file is not created, check your quotation marks, spacing, >, and filename.
06

STEP 6 OF 11

Read the file

Read the file you created with cat. This lets you verify that the text was written correctly.

TYPE THIS COMMAND

$cat New-File.txt

Then press Enter.

💡
Quick tip

Files are case sensitive. New-File.txt and new-file.txt can be treated as different names.

EXAMPLE — YOUR SCREEN MAY LOOK DIFFERENT
✓
WHAT YOU SHOULD SEE

The text you wrote into the file should appear directly below the command.

Having trouble?
If you see “No such file or directory,” run ls and check the exact filename.
07

STEP 7 OF 11

Remove the file

Remove only the practice file you created with rm.

⚠ Before you run thisThe rm command permanently removes the specified file. Only remove the practice file created in this tutorial.

TYPE THIS COMMAND

$rm New-File.txt

Then press Enter.

EXAMPLE — YOUR SCREEN MAY LOOK DIFFERENT
✓
WHAT YOU SHOULD SEE

There is usually no confirmation message. Run ls to verify that the file is gone.

Having trouble?
Double-check the filename. If rm says the file does not exist, use ls to find the correct name.
08

STEP 8 OF 11

Remove the directory

Return to the previous directory first. Then remove the empty practice directory. Run these as two separate commands.

⚠ Before you run thisBe careful with deletion commands. Confirm you are working only inside the tutorial environment.

1 — TYPE THIS COMMAND

$cd ..

Press Enter. This moves you out of New-Directory.

2 — THEN TYPE THIS COMMAND

$rmdir New-Directory

Press Enter again. This removes the now-empty directory.

💡
Quick tip

rmdir only removes empty directories.

EXAMPLE — YOUR SCREEN MAY LOOK DIFFERENT
✓
WHAT YOU SHOULD SEE

The directory should disappear from the listing after you verify with ls.

Having trouble?
If you see “Directory not empty,” make sure the file inside was removed first. If you are still inside the directory, use cd ...

Final challenge: find what is hidden

You have practiced the basics. Now use those skills to reveal a hidden file, recover its key, and display your completion certificate.

🔐
09

STEP 9 OF 11

Reveal the hidden file

Reveal hidden files with ls -a. Look for a filename that begins with a period (.); do not run that file.

TYPE THIS COMMAND

$ls -a

Then press Enter.

💡
Quick tip

The -a part is an option added to ls. It tells the command to show all files.

EXAMPLE — YOUR SCREEN MAY LOOK DIFFERENT
✓
WHAT YOU SHOULD SEE

A hidden file should now appear in the directory listing. Hidden files often begin with a period (.).

Having trouble?
If you still cannot find it, use pwd to confirm you are in the correct directory, then run ls -a again.
10

STEP 10 OF 11

Read the hidden file

Read the hidden file with cat, then copy the key displayed inside it. The hidden file itself is not a command; its contents contain the key you need for the final step.

TYPE THIS COMMAND

$cat [hidden-file-name]

Replace the entire [hidden-file-name] placeholder with the hidden filename you found in Step 9, including the period at the beginning. Do not type the square brackets. Then press Enter.

💡
What are you replacing?

Keep cat and the space after it. Delete [hidden-file-name] completely and type your hidden filename in its place. The text printed after you press Enter is the key; copy that text for Step 11.

EXAMPLE — YOUR SCREEN MAY LOOK DIFFERENT
✓
WHAT YOU SHOULD SEE

The file should display a key. Copy or carefully note that key—you will use it in the final step.

Having trouble?
If the file cannot be opened, use ls -a again and copy the hidden filename exactly, including the leading period.
11

STEP 11 OF 11

Use the key

Enter the key from Step 10 into the certificate command to display your completion message.

TYPE THIS COMMAND

$bash certificate.sh [your-key]

Replace the entire [your-key] placeholder with the key printed in Step 10. Do not type the square brackets. Then press Enter.

💡
What are you replacing?

Keep bash certificate.sh and the space after it. Delete [your-key] completely and type the exact key from Step 10 in its place.

EXAMPLE — YOUR SCREEN MAY LOOK DIFFERENT
EXAMPLE — YOUR SCREEN MAY LOOK DIFFERENT
Documents % bash certificate.sh [your-key]

WHAT YOU SHOULD SEE

If the key is correct, you should receive the special completion output from the program.

Having trouble?
If the certificate command fails, check the key for missing characters or extra spaces and try again.

💡 Helpful Tips & Examples

  • Commands and filenames are case sensitive.
  • Use pwd or ls if you are unsure where you are.
  • Use cd .. to move back one directory.
  • Press ↑ to cycle through recent commands.
  • rmdir only removes empty directories.
  • Type man [command] for the official manual page.

🔧 Troubleshooting

  • Command not working? Check spelling, capitalization, and spacing.
  • File not found? Confirm the filename and current directory.
  • Wrong directory? Use pwd, ls, and cd ...
  • Hidden file missing? Confirm your location, then run ls -a.

✓ Conclusion

Congratulations! You have practiced essential command-line skills for navigating directories, creating and reading files, cleaning up your workspace, and finding hidden content. These are foundational skills used throughout cybersecurity.
